clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant focal palmoplantar keratoderma with linear (striate) hyperkeratosis running along the palms and fingers and focal thickening on the soles
Caused by heterozygous variants in desmosomal genes, most often DSG1 (desmoglein 1) or DSP (desmoplakin), and occasionally KRT1
The linear pattern follows lines of mechanical stress, so the fingers and weight-bearing soles are typically involved
Because desmoplakin also functions in cardiac desmosomes, some DSP variants are associated with cardiocutaneous syndromes, so a cardiac history should be considered
Nails and hair are usually normal, helping to distinguish it from syndromic keratodermas
Diagnosis is clinical with family history; biopsy shows hyperkeratosis with widened intercellular spaces and can be supported by molecular testing
Management is supportive with keratolytics, emollients, mechanical paring and protective measures, with oral retinoids reserved for severe disease
reference.pathophysiology: Striate palmoplantar keratoderma results from haploinsufficiency or dominant-negative effects of variants in desmosomal proteins, chiefly desmoglein 1 and desmoplakin, which anchor keratin filaments to cell-cell junctions in the epidermis. Weakened desmosomal adhesion is most consequential in acral skin subjected to shearing and pressure, where impaired keratinocyte cohesion triggers compensatory hyperkeratosis along lines of mechanical stress, producing the characteristic striate pattern. Certain desmoplakin variants additionally impair cardiac desmosomes, linking the skin phenotype to arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy in some families.
additionalDifferentials: Focal palmoplantar keratoderma of pachyonychia congenita
Naxos disease and Carvajal syndrome (cardiocutaneous keratodermas)
Acquired keratoderma from friction or eczema
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of DSG1, DSP and related desmosomal genes
Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis with acantholytic-like widening of intercellular spaces
Cardiac assessment (history, ECG and echocardiography) where a DSP variant or cardiocutaneous syndrome is suspected
Nail and hair examination to exclude syndromic keratoderma
Clinical photography to document the striate pattern
redFlags: Personal or family history of arrhythmia, syncope or cardiomyopathy suggesting a cardiocutaneous desmoplakin syndrome
Woolly hair with keratoderma raising concern for Carvajal or Naxos syndrome
reference.prognosis: The cutaneous prognosis is good, with lifelong but manageable focal keratoderma; overall prognosis depends on excluding the cardiac involvement associated with some desmoplakin variants.
pitfalls: Failing to consider cardiac evaluation in desmoplakin-related disease
Confusing the linear pattern with a friction or occupational keratoderma
Overlooking woolly hair as a clue to a cardiocutaneous syndrome
Relying on systemic retinoids before optimising topical and mechanical care
